title: Each estimate either buys a box or rules one out
caption: Ask all four questions; several can be yes. Thresholds are rough single-node limits, not laws.

steps.text: Read load first. One database handles a few thousand reads/s comfortably; beyond ~10k/s, a cache (~100k ops/s per node) and read replicas take it.
Write load. Caches and replicas don't add write capacity; past what one primary can take, partition the data.
Size. Large binary objects go to object storage with only metadata in a DB; many TB of rows means sharding.
Bandwidth. Gigabits per second of the same static content belong at the edge, not on your servers.
All no? Say so: "one database and a couple of app servers handle this". That is a strong answer too.

scenarios.name: Photo app
scenarios.summary: Run the photo-app numbers through the questions: three of four say yes, and each yes is one box in the design.

steps.text: 17k peak reads/s > 10k: yes, so cache and replicas.
23 writes/s: no sharding. One primary is plenty.
5.5 PB of photos: yes, object storage for the bytes, metadata in the DB.
23 Gbps egress: yes, a CDN in front of the photo store.

scenarios.name: Internal tool
scenarios.summary: 5 000 employees, 50 req/s, 20 GB: every answer is no, and "one DB and two app servers" is the strong answer.

steps.text: A few writes/s and 20 GB of data: nothing to shard, nothing for blob storage.
Say it: keep it simple. Adding Kafka or a cache here would cost you points.

scenarios.name: Risk: averages only
scenarios.summary: Checking the average instead of the peak (5 800 vs 17 400 reads/s) answers no when it should be yes, and the design falls over at 8 pm.

steps.text: Use the average: 5 800 reads/s looks like one database can manage.
So the flowchart says keep it simple...
...but evening peak is 3× the average. 17 400 reads/s saturates the database exactly when most users are online.
Always multiply by the peak factor before asking the questions; then the cache is clearly needed.
